title: Taylor’s $4bn plan sits on shelf
full_text:
Angus Taylor is sitting on a fully costed policy plan that would raise more than $4bn over four years and help partly fund income tax cuts by allowing uncapped access for Australians to unlock up to 3 per cent of their superannuation annually in support of home ownership.
The Australian can reveal some members of Sussan Ley’s shadow expenditure review committee were earlier this year briefed on a super-for-housing plan and tax cuts package that would have been centrepieces of the former opposition leader’s first budget-in-reply speech. Amid anxiety in Coalition ranks about policy leaks to One Nation, which has released tobacco excise and superannuation policies in the past few weeks, Mr Taylor is under pressure from colleagues to go harder than Pauline Hanson on super for housing despite Labor claims the right-wing parties will destroy the super system.
Under Ms Ley’s plan, which was put on ice by Mr Taylor after he ousted her as leader in February, Australians could opt in and claim 3 per cent of the 12 per cent super guarantee through their employers via payroll wages.
Under this method, the marginal tax rate would have applied, rather than a concessional rate available through superannuation, and raised just over $1bn a year over the forward estimates. The revenue raised would have contributed to a tax cuts package that Ms Ley planned to unveil in her budget-in-reply address.
The policy design to distribute via payroll as wages was considered by senior Liberals as effective in nullifying expected Labor and industry super fund attacks that it was a “raid on super balances”.
The framing would have focused on workers withdrawing their employers’ money and securing higher wages rather than withdrawing directly from super accounts.
Coalition sources believe the policy would be easier to administer than One Nation’s capped model, which allows workers who are renting or paying a mortgage access to 3 per cent of their 12 per cent compulsory super contribution for a maximum of three years. The Ley model was uncapped and excluded renters.
Shadow ERC members under Ms Ley included current shadow cabinet ministers Tim Wilson, Andrew Bragg, Ted O’Brien, James Paterson and Anne Ruston, as well former Nationals leader David Littleproud and Kevin Hogan.
Senior Liberal sources said the policy was never formally taken to the shadow ERC and had been driven by Ms Ley’s office. While Ms Ley’s super-for-housing and income tax plans did not make it through the full shadow cabinet processes, individual shadow ministers were aware of the policy proposals and costings conducted by the Parliamentary Budget Office late last year.
A member of the committee said “this ambitious economic reform would have empowered Australians to immediately benefit from higher wages and lower tax brackets”. “When Australians earn more income the government generates more revenue, but the beauty of this policy is that this extra revenue would have been redirected into costed tax cuts,” the source said.
“The Morrison government was nuts to take the super guarantee from 9 to 12 and this would have fixed that public policy disaster while netting a real political dividend – more home ownership, higher wages, lower taxes.” Treasurer Jim Chalmers, who on Tuesday revealed he would release his second Intergenerational Report on September 21, said: “One Nation, the Liberals and the Nationals are indistinguishable when it comes to attacking wages, attacking super and attacking workers”.
“It’s another reminder that this side of the House backs Australian workers, that side just attacks them,” Dr Chalmers said during question time. “Those opposite are all anti-super, because they are all anti-worker.” Senator Bragg, the opposition housing spokesman, on Tuesday said “the biggest problem we have in this country now in the retirement system is the growing trend of retired renters. If we are going to become almost a majority nation of retired renters, then we need to look very carefully at how these things are calibrated. The Retirement Income Review itself found that the key determinant of your success in retirement was your housing status. If that is slipping away, then it is reckless and crazy for the Labor Party to say that nothing can be improved, everything is perfect.” Asked if the Coalition was gazumped by One Nation on the super policy, Senator Bragg said “we always have the usual policy reviews and internal processes that you would expect in a democracy to be undertaken”.
“My colleagues are very focused on policy … they are wanting, they are ambitious and hungry for policy, and that’s what we’ve been doing,” he said.
“We’ve announced policies last week; we’ve announced policies in the budget reply. It’s an ongoing process, and I know that we’re all committed to that.” Ahead of the 2022 election, Scott Morrison announced that a re-elected Coalition government would enable first-home buyers to use up to 40 per cent of their super, up to $50,000, to help buy a home.
Peter Dutton and Mr Taylor were accused of failing to effectively differentiate their housing policies from Labor’s offerings ahead of last year’s federal election.
